cases.abstract: We introduce Equivariant Diffusion Policy, which constrains action denoising to respect planar rotations in manipulation. For an SO(2)-equivariant expert, transforming observations and noisy actions together also transforms the target noise, provided noise follows the action representation. This relationship motivates imposing symmetry on the noise predictor itself. We derive rotation representations for absolute and relative SE(3) gripper commands, then connect equivariant observation and action encoders to a decoder through a temporal U-Net with parameters shared across discrete rotations. The construction respects the different transformation rules of absolute and relative control. Across 12 MimicGen tasks, voxel-input absolute control with 200 demonstrations averages 72.6% peak success over training, exceeding the strongest baseline average with 1,000 demonstrations (71.4%); simulation results average training maxima across three seeds. On six physical-robot tasks with 20-60 demonstrations, success ranges from 80% to 95%, compared with 0%-60% for a similarly sized non-equivariant policy using the same voxels. Benefits are larger in low-data simulation settings, while gains diminish at larger data budgets and sensing can violate the assumed symmetry.
cases.results: Matching the visual representation on hardware shows that the gains are not explained solely by voxel input. With 20-60 demonstrations per task, EquiDiff succeeds in 80%-95% of trials across six tasks, versus 0%-60% for a non-equivariant diffusion policy using the same voxel grid and approximately the same parameter count; each policy receives 20 trials per task. On letter alignment, the contrast is 19/20 versus 0/20. Simulation provides complementary evidence at limited data: with 100 demonstrations and absolute control, the RGB version averages 53.7% success across 12 tasks, compared with 42.0% for DiffPo-C using the same observation type and temporal U-Net backbone. These simulation values average the maximum success over 50 evaluations during training across three seeds. The absolute-control RGB advantage is smaller with more demonstrations, and relative-control RGB gains over the strongest baseline are modest. Together, the comparisons support symmetry-aware denoising under restricted demonstration budgets without attributing the gains simply to a richer visual input.

cases.abstract: Robot dataset curation must distinguish domains that offer useful learning progress from those with high imitation loss simply because they are noisy or difficult. We introduce Re-Mix, which learns domain weights through group distributionally robust optimization on loss relative to a reference policy, rather than raw loss. Gaussian normalization aligns action scales across heterogeneous domains, action discretization avoids reliance on outlier-sensitive continuous losses, and early stopping keeps reference losses from collapsing through memorization. Re-Mix returns reusable weights rather than a final policy: weights learned with discrete action models guide both diffusion-policy training and data retention without target-task information. Evaluation uses WidowX and Franka robots, with a 5% in-domain co-training mixture because pretraining alone fails to transfer to the evaluation setups. On RT-X, learned weights outperform uniform and expert-designed mixtures and retain reported performance after reducing the dataset to 25%. On quarter-sized Bridge V2, mean success is 90%, versus 50% for uniform subsetting and 22% for visual-embedding selection. Full-data Bridge weighting produces little difference, showing that the value of curation depends on the data regime.
cases.results: Bridge V2 distinguishes improving a mixture from deciding which data can be removed. Learned scene weights and uniform sampling perform similarly on the full dataset's two evaluation tasks. With only 25% retained, however, Re-Mix averages 90% success across four tasks, compared with 50% for uniform subsetting and 22% for Self-Supervised Prototypes, which selects for diversity in visual embeddings. Each task receives 10 physical trials. The final diffusion policies use the same 400,000-step training budget and a 5% co-training mixture containing 25 in-domain demonstrations for each of three tasks. Thus, the subset comparison favors action-informed curation at matched retained volume, rather than more data or training steps. Retention and training-time domain weights change together, so this tests their combined effect. RT-X similarly retains reported performance under Re-Mix subsetting while expert-weighted subsetting loses performance. Since Bridge subsetting adds two tasks, its full-data and quarter-data averages are not paired measurements of the same task set.
